title: We’re Teaching Students to Game the Tests
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Kane, a new fifth grade teacher, uses his district's online DIBELS MAZE comprehension assessment to argue that digital testing is training students to guess their way through school. After his team saw many students clicking through the online test without effort, they agreed to try the paper version. He points to the testing industry's own research on mode effects, which shows students score lower on digital versions and leads test makers to lower cut scores to compensate. His concern is less about data validity than about habits: in an era of state tests, benchmark tests and progress monitoring, lower-achieving students in particular learn to treat assessments like a video game to be finished fast. The NWEA MAP rapid-guessing detector illustrates the point, since students simply learn to guess slowly. He proposes fewer tests tied to clear next steps, given mostly on paper, with less pressure on districts to maintain fleets of devices.
points: Test makers already lower cut scores on digital versions to compensate for the fact that students do worse on screens.
Kane observes that guessing is concentrated among lower-achieving students, for whom screens reduce the friction to giving up.
MAP's rapid-guessing detector teaches students not to try harder but to pause between guesses.
He argues the real cost of constant digital testing is the habit it builds, not the noise in the data.
His alternative is fewer, paper-based assessments linked to clear instructional next steps.
quotes: I asked if there was a paper and pencil option. The trainer seemed taken aback. Well, there is...but why would you want to do that?
One of the things they learned is what they call a “mode effect,” which is a fancy way of saying that kids do worse on digital tests.
But there’s something about screens that reduces the friction to guessing, that brings in the habits students develop playing video games or fiddling with apps, swiping on to the next thing.
All these tests aren’t neutral. Students are building habits, and for more and more students all the tests seem silly so they build a habit of guessing their way through.
And what they learn is not that they should try their best. They learn that they need to guess slowly. Guess. Pause. Stare into space for a minute. Guess again. Repeat.
My concern is what we’re training students for. Students should come to school to learn. Students should not come to school to practice gaming tests they don’t care about.
Here’s what I’m imagining: fewer tests, with each test linked to clear outcomes and next steps for teachers based on the data.
